# **Ethical Considerations**
***

There are some important ethical considerations when working with version control, as well as with health-related data in general and when collaborating on scientific projects. 

1. When hosting data, code, and results on {{< glossary "GitHub">}}, **make sure to never include personally identifiable information (PII) or protected health information (PHI) in a repository**. This includes names, dates of birth, medical records and diagnosis, lab results, identifiable genomic sequencing data, as well as other types of data. You can read more about PII and PHI in [this course](https://hutchdatascience.org/Ethical_Data_Handling_for_Cancer_Research/data-privacy.html#pii-personal-identifiable-information) about ethical data handling. For more general information about data management, you can explore [this course](https://hutchdatascience.org/Proactive_Data_Management_and_Sharing/). 

    a. Private repositories prevent other GitHub users from viewing your repository and are therefore useful when you are not yet ready to share your work publicly. However, private repositories are **not an appropriate place to store PII or PHI**. While versions of [GitHub Enterprise](https://github.com/enterprise) may offer additional security and administrative controls, the ability to store sensitive data depends on institutional policies, compliance requirements, and contractual agreements. Unless you have explicit guidance from your institution approving such use, you should assume that PII and PHI should not be stored in GitHub repositories.

    a. If you do commit sensitive information (PHI or PII) to a version controlled repository on GitHub, it is **not sufficient to simply remove the file, commit the changes, and push again**. If you do this, any files with sensitive information will be part of a commit, and will therefore be a part of the history of the repository. While there are ways to remove sensitive information from a local commit, and from a GitHub repository, these procedures are more complicated and may disrupt workflows for other collaborators working on the repository. It is important to inform collaborators of the sensitive information that has been committed.
  
1. It is important to carefully review files before staging and committing changes to ensure you aren't pushing anything sensitive to GitHub, such as credentials, keys, access tokens, passwords, etc. Some tools automatically create environmental files containing credentials (these files have names like ".env"). Make sure that these files are included in your .gitignore and are never staged, committed, or pushed to GitHub. 
1. Make sure to keep comprehensive documentation for scientific projects to avoid losing track of which data generated a set of results or figure, or which version of a software you used in an analysis. Version control can help you do this. Reproducible science is ethical science: without a transparent and well-documented process, others in the scientific community cannot easily verify or trust your results.
1. For projects with large teams, it can be challenging to track individual contributions. {{< glossary "Version control">}} histories can be helpful to see who worked on each component on an analysis, in order to fairly acknowledge each contributor’s work. You can read [this paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11948-014-9562-8) for more ethical considerations related to large team science. 
1. When performing a {{< glossary "meta-analysis">}} such as the one described in this case study, it is important to be transparent about inclusion and exclusion criteria for studies and for individual observations within studies. Criteria should be determined before analysis, to avoid choosing studies that will support a desired conclusion. It is also important to properly cite the original studies and recognize the groups that collected the data.
